questions.q: Identify two examples of non-standard or colloquial grammar used by the Tiger King in the poem and state the grammatical rule each violates in standard English.
questions.a: Examples: "gonna" (violates standard "going to" future construction) and "I've got it all planned" where "got" replaces "have" as main verb (violates standard "I have got" or "I've gotten" in formal usage). A wrong answer (e.g., citing "He cramps our style" as non-standard) reveals the student confuses idiomatic phrasing with grammatical deviation; "cramps" is standard verb usage.

questions.q: Explain why the poet uses direct speech for the Tiger King's lines ("'That's shocking,' said the tiger king. 'Why didn't you come to see me before?'") but shifts to indirect narrative for the sheep dog's actions ("The sheep dog was the type who had never told a lie in his life"). What grammatical difference in reporting creates this effect?
questions.a: Direct speech uses quoted exact words with reporting clause ("said the tiger king") preserving the speaker's voice, tense, and colloquialisms. Indirect narrative reports actions/thoughts in third-person past tense ("was the type who had never told") without quotation marks, creating narrative distance. A wrong answer focusing only on "one is dialogue, one isn't" misses the grammatical shift: direct speech retains original tense/pronouns; indirect shifts them (e.g., "I have never lied" → "he had never told a lie").

questions.q: In the line "He kept on making frantic signs. But Ajamil, the good shepherd, refused to meet his eyes," rewrite the second sentence beginning with "Refusing to meet his eyes..." using a participle phrase. Explain how this change alters the focus.
questions.a: "Refusing to meet his eyes, Ajamil, the good shepherd, ..." The participle phrase front-shifts the action, making Ajamil's deliberate avoidance the grammatical subject of the main clause, emphasizing his complicity. A student who writes "Ajamil refused to meet his eyes, refusing..." creates a dangling modifier or redundancy, showing they don't grasp how participle placement shifts thematic weight.

questions.q: Compare the sentence structures in the opening stanza ("The tiger people went to their king / and said, 'We're starving...'") and the closing stanza ("He is free to play a flute all day / as well fed tigers and fat sheep drink from the same pond..."). Analyze how the shift from compound sentences with coordinate clauses to a complex sentence with subordinate clause ("as...") reflects the poem's thematic resolution.
questions.a: Opening uses parataxis (coordinate "and") showing fragmented, desperate pleas—each clause equal, mirroring chaotic petitioning. Closing uses hypotaxis ("as" introducing cause/condition) showing integrated, controlled outcome: the shepherd's syntax now subordinates nature to his design. A wrong answer listing sentence types without linking to power dynamics misses the analytical leap: grammar enacts the political shift from disorder to manipulated order.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the poet's use of the contraction "won't" in "He cramps our style / and won't let us get within a mile / of meat" versus the full form "will not." Consider tone, rhythm, and character.
questions.a: "won't" creates conversational, aggrieved tone matching the tigers' petty complaint; its single syllable keeps the anapestic rhythm ("and WON'T let us GET..."). "will not" would sound formal, authoritative—undermining the tigers' portrayal as whining supplicants. A student claiming "no difference" ignores how phonological reduction signals register; a student saying "it's just informal" misses the metrical function.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in the poem's style where a corrupt official justifies a bribe, using at least two colloquial contractions, one sentence fragment, and one elliptical construction (omitted subject/auxiliary). Label each feature.
questions.a: Sample: "'Gotta feed the fam,' the minister winked, / 'Rules? Bent, not broken—ask anyone.' / Pocket lined. / 'Just how the system runs.'" Features: "Gotta" (colloquial contraction), "Bent, not broken" (fragment), "ask anyone" (imperative elliptical for "you ask anyone"), "Pocket lined" (elliptical "His pocket [was] lined"). A poor answer uses standard grammar throughout or misses the satirical voice, showing inability to replicate grammatical characterization.
